item.title: NASCAR's most popular driver has a TikTok girlfriend that's causing a stir, and he doesn't care
item.description: Carson Hocevar leads NASCAR merchandise sales and has a TikTok girlfriend, but Denny Hamlin and Kevin Harvick say he needs to focus on racing.
item.content:encoded:
Carson Hocevar isn't your typical NASCAR driver. He's not your daddy's driver.

He's certainly not your granddaddy's driver.

He's no Dale Earnhardt. He's not Richard Petty or Cale Yarborough or, for those looking for a more recent driver, Tony Stewart.

In a way, he's probably the closest thing to Jeff Gordon we've had since ... Jeff Gordon.

CARSON HOCEVAR SAYS HIS MOM WAS MORE FIRED UP ABOUT HIM GOING TO THE MET GALA THAN WINNING AT TALLADEGA

Hocevar, 23, is rewriting the rules in just about every single way. He's only got one career Cup win — earlier this year at Talladega (hey, maybe he is Dale!) — but is currently leading the series in merchandise sales.

Last year, he wasn't even in the Top 30.

When I told my wife I was interviewing Carson Hocevar earlier this week, I expected her to look at me like I had three heads.

"Oh, I know him," she said. "From TikTok."

"I just kind of laugh about it," Hocevar said about all the attention — both good and bad — he's getting from a suddenly vibrant social media presence.

"You know, the night before Talladega, I was six hours away at my buddy's place driving $500 cars, and then we win the next day. So, you know, it's always ... you just put yourself in that spot sometimes that I think in racing, when people just want to have a reason for stuff, they don't want to just be like, 'Oh, circumstance, you know?'

"They just want to dictate a reason or, you know, push a story or whatever."

Hocevar's popularity, both within the sport and outside of it, has exploded this summer. In July, social media sleuths started linking him to popular influencer, Tabitha Swatosh.

Swatosh has over 15 million followers on TikTok, and unleashed a video last month that tallied nearly 500,000 likes.

"A NASCAR man invited me to be his date to an event," she said in the video before showing all 15 million followers how she gets ready for said event.

Side note: No, I don't get it. Don't ask me why people watch what they watch on TikTok. I have no clue. I'm not the target audience, though.

Anyway, fast-forward a few weeks, and the two were spotting together on the starting grid before the Indianapolis 500.

Pretty easy to connect the dots after this:

Which brings us to August, where Carson finished 31st, 37th, 19th and, after a late crash last Saturday at Daytona, 38th.

Not great!

Add in some off-the-track drama around Swatosh after she "wore heels to a race," which apparently didn't sit well with some fans, and it's been a rocky summer for Hocevar.

Too much TikTok girlfriend and not enough practice in the simulator? Well, if you ask championship favorite Denny Hamlin ...

"I don't know. It just was not a very good day," Hamlin said about Hocevar on his 'Actions Detrimental' podcast following a wreck at New Hampshire.

"The best thing that's come out of that camp in a month is his girl's tutorial on makeup and racing."

Whoooooooof.

Hamlin wasn't alone.

"Here’s how it goes a lot of times when you see a young driver that gets a lot of attention, had some success, wins a race," former Cup champion Kevin Harvick said last week. "Got a TikTok girlfriend. All these things that go along with all that, and then they forget that they need to drive the freaking race car. 

"The guy can drive the crap out of the race car, and all the other stuff is really cool ... No one cares if your car is not fast. It does not matter if you don’t have the results.

"They will forget about you in weeks."

There's certainly some truth to that. Fans want to root for a winner. Hocevar told me as much when I spoke to him earlier this week.

But if you win, and nobody knows anything else about you, that probably won't last, either.

"A lot of my friends love the WWE and they they were reading the WWE Reddit, and they're in some of the comments and they thought they accidentally switched to the NASCAR Reddit by accident because the fans over there kind of say the same stuff they do over here," Hocevar said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"They don't understand the new guys. 'This guy is popular, and I don't understand why.' A lot of my friends, some of them love WWE and all the intricacies of that world. But the casuals of it, they're like, 'Man, I loved Stone Cold when he walked out. I never even watched him wrestle, but I liked him, and the Undertaker and their shticks.

"It's very similar to how NASCAR fans describe everything and become negative to everything. A lot of times, they're not sure what they're looking for."

NASCAR, by the way, is sure what it's looking for.

The series has been pushing Hocevar over the past few weeks in a way we haven't seen ... maybe ever?

Last Thursday, the series sent out a press release titled, "Does Everyone Hate Carson Hocevar?" It was odd. You don't see that in this business.

The story made sure to note that Hocevar is currently No. 1 driver in retail sales on the NASCAR Shop website, and ranked inside the top five of trackside sales.

He was No. 32 this time last season.

"Love him or hate him, Carson Hocevar is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore … so catch him and all his enemies this Saturday night, Aug. 29, during the Coke Zero Sugar 400," the article concluded.

So, yeah — NASCAR isn't oblivious to this. They're very clearly pushing Carson Hocevar to the center of the table, and letting the chips fall where they may.

There's a reason I spoke to Carson earlier this week. I didn't ask. He was offered. That also doesn't happen often.

It's not the worst strategy in the world. Every sport needs a villain. A lightning rod. Someone who's going to move the needle.

NASCAR, in particular, has been desperate for that driver for a decade now. Jeff Gordon retired in 2015. Tony Stewart retired in 2016. Dale Earnhardt Jr. retired in 2017.

Kyle Busch, sadly, died in May. He was undoubtedly the most polarizing driver in the sport for years. His death rocked the series in more ways than one.

So now, apparently, it's Carson Hocevar's turn.

He's got the TikTok girlfriend, as Kevin Harvick said. The social media presence. Plenty of enemies on the track. He's also got a shot at winning a Cup championship in a few months.

The only thing left to do?

Win.

"I've had people try to wreck me and they just end up wrecking themselves lately," Hocevar said with a smile, referring to Zane Smith's move at Chicagoland in July. "I think we'll just enjoy these (next) ten (races) and keep working and, you know, just see where it works out."

item.title: Scottie Scheffler's caddie details conversation about potential $1 billion LIV Golf offer, why he'd decline
item.description: Caddie Ted Scott reveals Scottie Scheffler's bold response when asked about a potential $250 million LIV Golf offer as the world's top player.
item.content:encoded:
Scottie Scheffler recently took over the top spot on the PGA Tour's career money list with more than $130 million earned. It's fair to say that the 30-year-old who has already taken home $10 million more than Tiger Woods did in his career is doing just fine financially, but as his caddie, Ted Scott, recently explained, it's not all about the money for Scheffler.

Scheffler became the No. 1 player in the world in March 2022, amid LIV Golf's efforts to lure players away from the PGA Tour, and just three months before the then Saudi-backed circuit's inaugural event.

Scott began caddying for Scheffler in November 2021, and having been in the partnership for less than six months at the time, he was still very much in the feeling-things-out stage with his new boss, but one conversation very much set the tone.

"When I first started working for him, he was 19th in the world, and he had a white golf bag," Scott said, referring to Scheffler, on a recent appearance on PGA Tour Radio. "I didn't know him that well, and I asked him, I was like: 'Why don't you have sponsors?'

"He's like, 'Well, because I just want to play with the equipment that I want to play.' And I was like, 'Okay.' And then I remember whenever all the LIV stuff was going on, you know, he was number one in the world at the time, I didn't know, but I said, 'They're probably going to offer you like $250m to go over there.'

"And he says, 'I don't care what they offer me. They can offer me a billion dollars. I'm going to play where the best players are because I just want to beat people.'"

Scott went on to admit that it was at that moment he realized just how differently Scheffler is wired.

While Scott already had a stellar resume as a caddie before joining forces with Scheffler, having been on the bag for both of Bubba Watson's Masters victories, he and Scheffler have turned into a two-headed monster over the last half-decade.

Scott has been on the bag for each of Scheffler's 22 PGA Tour wins, dating back to his first in February 2022, plus the four major championships Scheffler has won at this point in his young career.

Scheffler earned just shy of $31 million on the PGA Tour in 2026. With caddies typically earning around 10 percent of a player's earnings, on the low end, Scott likely earned well over $3 million this past season on Tour.

item.title: The privacy risk of moving to a retirement community
item.description: Moving to a 55+ community can quickly expose your data to scammers and data brokers before you even unpack, putting your whole family at risk.
item.content:encoded:
The moving truck hasn't even left the driveway. Somewhere, a scammer may already know three things about you: your name, your new address and something about your age. Maybe not your exact age, but potentially enough information to make you a more attractive target.

Federal law sets specific rules for communities that qualify as housing for people 55 and older. One requirement says at least 80% of occupied units must house at least one person who is 55 or older. Those requirements come from the Housing for Older Persons Act.

That means an address inside a known 55+ community can give scammers and data brokers another clue about you. Once public records connect your name to that address, data brokers can add it to a much larger profile.

That is the part nobody mentions in the moving checklist. Here is how that profile can come together so quickly. More importantly, here is how you can reduce the personal information scammers can find.

FIVE DATA BROKER OPT-OUT MYTHS THAT LEAVE RETIREES EXPOSED

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Moving into an age-restricted community does more than change your ZIP Code. It can quickly create a new, highly concentrated data profile.

Here's what can become available:

Each detail may seem harmless by itself. However, scammers can combine those details to build a convincing profile of you.

SELLING YOUR HOME? YOUR DATA IS ALREADY MOVING

Criminologists at Florida State University spent years studying financial exploitation inside a large Florida retirement community. Their findings should change how you think about your first few months in a new home. Residents told researchers that scammers targeted them immediately and repeatedly after they moved into the retirement community. They also faced scams far more often than before their move.

One of the study's authors, Julie Brancale, told AARP that residents faced targeting almost immediately after moving in. She said the attempts then continued. Her colleague, Thomas Blomberg, described another problem. People may move into gated communities expecting greater safety during retirement. Instead, they can face repeated scam attempts.

AARP's reporting on The Villages also highlights real cases of financial exploitation. The Villages is the country's largest 55+ community and has more than 150,000 residents. For example, a pair posing as pool contractors allegedly collected nearly $200,000 in down payments from six residents. Police later arrested them. A Leisure World resident in Maryland lost close to $800,000 in a gold-bar scam. Meanwhile, one local anti-fraud group estimates that it has recovered roughly $40 million for Florida victims over the years.

Here's the part that should get your attention. When a scammer searches for information about you, your adult children may appear too. Data broker profiles may list them as relatives and connect them to current addresses. As a result, a scam aimed at a new resident can spread to the whole family.

A criminal may never need to trick you directly. For example, someone could call your daughter and pretend to represent your new HOA. The caller could mention your real address and ask her to confirm a payment on your behalf. That request can sound convincing because the caller already knows personal details. The more information criminals collect beforehand, the easier they can make a fake story sound believable.

This problem reaches far beyond individual retirement communities. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than 201,000 fraud complaints from Americans 60 and older in 2025. Those complaints totaled more than $7.7 billion in reported losses.

The FTC estimates that the true financial impact could reach as high as $81.5 billion after accounting for unreported cases. An analysis of FBI complaint data also found another troubling link. Roughly 72% of fraud categories affecting older adults can become more dangerous when attackers have access to personal information.

The takeaway is simple. Personal information gives scammers material they can use to make a fraudulent call, text or email sound more believable.

THE ONE THING SCAMMERS CHECK BEFORE TARGETING YOU ONLINE

You cannot prevent every county property record from becoming public. However, you can reduce how much additional information someone finds once they start looking.

First, ask your HOA or community manager whether you can limit or opt out of resident directory listings. Also, ask what information the community shares with other residents. If possible, remove your phone number, email address and photo from community directories.

Next, search your name, phone number and new address online to see what appears. People-search sites and data brokers may already connect your new location with your age range, relatives and previous addresses.

Remove your information from data broker sites

You can submit removal requests directly to people-search sites and data brokers that list your information, but doing it yourself can take a lot of time and effort. A data removal service can handle those requests on your behalf and continue checking whether your information reappears. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Moving into a 55+ community can create a privacy risk earlier than many people realize. What concerns me most is how quickly your new address can become connected to your age range, relatives and other personal details across public records and data broker sites.

The Florida State University research really stands out to me because residents reported scam attempts soon after moving. To me, that means privacy needs to be part of your moving checklist before you unpack the boxes, not something you think about after suspicious calls start coming in.

I would also pay close attention to what your information reveals about your family. Data broker profiles often connect relatives, previous addresses and household details. That gives scammers more ways to make a fake story sound convincing to you or someone close to you.

With Americans 60 and older reporting more than $7.7 billion in fraud losses to the FBI in 2025, I would not wait for a scam attempt to start protecting your information. Search for your name and address online, ask what your community shares and remove personal data from broker sites wherever possible.

item.title: Photographer hit in head with hard foul ball at Yankees-Angels game, carted off in scary scene
item.description: Ben Rice's hard foul ball struck a photographer in the camera well at Angel Stadium, halting the New York Yankees-Los Angeles Angels game for about 10 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
During the sixth inning of the New York Yankees’ 6-3 extra-inning win over the Los Angeles Angels on Wednesday, a scary scene unfolded when a photographer was hit in the head by a hard foul ball.

The photographer was sitting in the camera well on the first-base side of Angel Stadium when Yankees designated hitter Ben Rice yanked Angels starting pitcher Reid Detmers' 87-mph slider foul into the camera well. The ball came off Rice’s bat at 79.5 mph, and the All-Star slugger knew something was wrong immediately and had a concerned look on his face.

The Yankees medical staff quickly sprang into action as Mike Schuck, the director of sports medicine and rehab, jumped into the well to tend to the injured photographer. Tim Lentych, the Yankees' head trainer, called for a cart to come out.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The game was delayed for about 10 minutes as the cart came out for the photographer, with the crowd remaining silent. Rice walked away from the batter’s box and over to the camera well to watch the emergency medical staff tend to the photographer.

The photographer eventually walked off under his own power, with a neck brace on, and made it to the cart. Rice shook hands with the photographer before returning to the batter’s box.

An Angels spokesperson relayed through the photographer’s outlet that he was OK and receiving medical attention, according to the New York Post.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"Very relieved," Rice said, according to the New York Post. "I saw it, he definitely was not ready for any kind of impact there, he was looking the other direction."

"I wasn’t sure how square it hit him in the head, but definitely a scary scene, so happy to hear he’s OK."

Once the at-bat resumed, Detmers induced a flyout to center field from Rice on the ninth pitch of the at-bat.

Rice had two hits and an RBI in five at-bats in the team’s win.

item.title: Musk picks his first GOP warriors as a 2026 money surge takes shape
item.description: America PAC spent over $800,000 in 12 days backing Republicans, with Ken Paxton's Texas Senate race receiving the largest share of Elon Musk's cash.
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk’s super PAC made its first major publicly disclosed burst of midterm spending, dumping significant amounts of cash over a very short period of time into races Republicans virtually must win to retain control of Congress.

Between Aug. 19 and Aug. 31, Musk’s America PAC reported just over $800,000 in expenditures supporting Republican candidates and opposing their Democratic rivals — an average of roughly $70,000 per day. By far the largest concentration of Musk’s spending was in the Texas Senate race, where America PAC spent nearly $248,000 supporting Paxton and opposing Talarico.

Republicans are heading into the midterms with a massive cash advantage, but are struggling to secure advantageous positions in even traditionally Republican states such as Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Ohio, according to Fox News’ Power Rankings. Musk opening his pocketbook for the GOP, an eventuality that was once in doubt given his prior split with the president, could provide Republicans with a much-needed lifeline as November approaches.

JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH'

The bulk of the spending went toward "printing" expenses paid out to Storytellers Group, a political vendor that specializes in direct-mail work.

Over his 12-day expenditure period, Musk spent $123,000 opposing Talarico’s candidacy and about $125,000 supporting Paxton, according to a campaign finance filing released Wednesday.

RNC CHAIR SAYS TALARICO'S GOP CROSSOVER HOPES ARE A 'PIPE DREAM': 'NOBODY IS GOING TO FOLLOW HIM'

The spending, while helpful to Republicans, gives Democrats a new angle of attack to use in the districts where Musk’s PAC is deploying resources. Musk has suffered from low favorability ratings among Americans, and his efforts with the Department of Government Efficiency, likewise, proved unpopular.

Democrats running in the competitive races where Musk is spending can now credibly tie their opponents to the billionaire. Talarico, for instance, has made running against billionaire interests a focal point of his campaign, a plank that increases in relevance now that Musk has waded into his race.

AFTER PLATNER IMPLOSION, MAINE DEMOCRATS RUSH TOWARD NEW SENATE NOMINEE DESPITE FRESH WARNING SIGNS

Musk’s PAC also spent a considerable amount in Maine’s Senate race, deploying roughly $135,000 against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson and about $35,000 to assist incumbent GOP Sen. Susan Collins. Collins has worked to distance herself from the Trump administration and national Republicans as she seeks re-election in a left-leaning state, an effort Musk’s spending could complicate.

Other races Musk’s PAC spent in include the Senate races in Michigan, Ohio and New Hampshire as well as a handful of competitive House races in states like New York, Florida and Wisconsin.

GOP donors, fundraisers and lawmakers are worried that their current cash advantage may not be enough to deliver victory in November. They worry that President Donald Trump may not deploy his $400 million political war chest aggressively enough.

item.title: Alanis Morissette sues ex-tour manager over alleged blackmail, false drug trafficking claims
item.description: Alanis Morissette claimed her former tour manager threatened to frame her for drug trafficking at a U.K. airport unless she agreed to a 15-year contract.
item.content:encoded:
Alanis Morissette claimed to be the victim of a "calculated blackmail campaign" allegedly orchestrated by her "disgruntled former tour manager," according to court documents obtained by Fox News Digital.

The "Ironic" singer accused Keren Urinov of civil extortion in a lawsuit filed Tuesday, and claimed her ex-manager attempted to frame her for drug trafficking at an airport in the United Kingdom.

"While temporarily employed to manage a Morissette tour, Urinov admitted to the British Border Force that a bag seized at an airport that allegedly contained marijuana and xylazine belonged to her," the documents stated.

RAPPER FACES $2.8M LAWSUIT AFTER AXING OPENING ACT FROM TOUR FOLLOWING HER POLITICAL RANT

"Urinov now threatens to report to the British authorities that Morissette committed drug trafficking unless Morissette agrees to employ her as a tour director for fifteen years and pay her massive compensation."

The Canadian singer allegedly hired Urinov in 2025 to serve as her temporary tour manager. In July 2025, Morissette and her team were scheduled to fly from Farnborough Airport in the U.K. to Spain for a concert.

"At the airport, a British Border Force official flagged a bag for further inspection and asked who owned the bag. Urinov said the bag was hers," the documents stated.

Urinov allegedly told the team that the Border Force "had arrested her and issued her a seizure notice alleging that the bag contained marijuana and xylazine" after she admitted the bag belonged to her.

"Urinov showed the Border Force her Israeli medical marijuana license. The Border Force returned the bag to Urinov and released her," the lawsuit stated.

BLAKE LIVELY ALLEGES ‘MEAN GIRL’ SMEAR CAMPAIGN DAMAGED HER CAREER, SEEKS UP TO $296M

The following day, the touring team flew back to the United Kingdom, and upon landing, Urinov was once again detained and re-affirmed ownership of the bag and the alleged drugs inside.

"After the tour ended, Urinov and her attorney sent a series of increasingly extortionate letters to Morissette," documents stated. "Urinov threatened to file a patently frivolous lawsuit against Morissette in the United Kingdom for unspecified claims if Morissette refused to tell British law enforcement that the alleged drugs were hers."

She continued, "However, Urinov communicated, Morissette could put ‘an end to the matter’ by entering into a fixed-term, full-time employment contract of fifteen years with Urinov, under which Urinov would receive an income equivalent to that of a tour director with annual increases and bonuses."

Morissette claimed that Urinov also demanded that she arrange for an immigration attorney to obtain a work visa that would allow Urinov to work in the U.S. A demand for additional compensation was relayed if the visa could not be obtained.

"Morissette is not interested in employing Urinov for fifteen years—not only because she is a blackmailer, but also because she was a terrible manager of the 2025 tour," documents stated.

The "You Oughta Know" singer claimed Urinov made an "inexplicable error" in hotel bookings that allegedly cost the singer $70,000.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Also while on tour, "Urinov told Morissette’s team that law enforcement in a Latin American country had arrested her and a friend several years ago for smuggling drugs in a surfboard," documents stated.

"Urinov explained that she had illegally fled the country after being released on bail. This was an astounding revelation, given that Urinov had told Morissette’s team during her interview for the tour manager position that nothing in her past would cause any complications with obtaining visas or traveling, and she never mentioned her arrest or crimes in Latin America."

Morissette sued Urinov for civil extortion, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, and in addition to a jury trial, requested compensatory damages "of an amount in excess of $75,000 in damages."

item.title: 33 House Dems break with Jeffries as party fractures over Israel
item.description: The House passed a bill to cut federal funds to colleges participating in boycotts of Israel, but Democrats argue it violates free speech rights.
item.content:encoded:
The House of Representatives passed a bill aimed at blocking federal funds to colleges that boycott Israel, with the vast majority of Democrats voting against it.

All but 33 left-wing lawmakers voted to block the measure, which would "prohibit an institution that participates in a non-expressive commercial boycott of Israel" from getting government funding. It would also force universities that do get federal funds to affirm their students "are not unreasonably obstructed" from studying abroad in Israel.

The measure passed 237 to 169, with all but two Republicans voting in favor. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and his top deputies were among the 167 Democrats to vote "no" alongside Reps. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Warren Davidson, R-Ohio.

It comes as antisemitism continues to be a growing threat in the U.S. amid Israel's war in Gaza.

CHAOS ERUPTS AS HOUSE PASSES $1.15T DEFENSE BILL WITH ISRAEL PROVISION: 'STOP STOKING JEW HATRED'

Democrats have argued the bill is an infringement on the First Amendment, while Republicans hold it up as a way to ensure Jewish students feel safe at U.S. colleges and universities.

Republicans have seized on Democrats' divisions on the issue, which has coincided with a far-left insurgency plunging the party into civil war ahead of the midterms.

HOUSE DEMOCRATS FRACTURE BADLY OVER MASSIE AMENDMENT TO CUT $3.3B IN U.S. AID TO ISRAEL

Far-left Democrats, like the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), have attacked members of their own party who they view as not sufficiently critical of Israel. It's translated into some antisemitic incidents, such as a gay Jewish Democrat running for Congress in California getting run out of a pro-transgender rights march over his support for Israel's sovereignty.

Scott Wiener told CNN that people in the crowd made references to his "Israeli handlers" while berating him, a well-worn antisemitic trope.

DEM RUNNING FOR PELOSI’S SEAT MOCKED AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL HECKLERS CHASE HIM FROM SF TRANS MARCH

Those divisions were present on Thursday morning as well, with Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., co-leading the legislation that his own senior Democratic leadership opposed.

Gottheimer said of the legislation in a statement, "The goal of the BDS movement is the destruction of the democratic State of Israel, America’s critical ally in the global fight against terror. BDS has no place on college campuses or anywhere in our country. At a time when our Jewish students are facing death threats, being physically assaulted, and blocked from going to class simply for who they are, we must do everything possible to ensure they can learn safely, speak freely, and get the education they deserve."

But progressives, including Rep. Jerry Nadler, D-N.Y., who said he otherwise opposes the boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel, called it an attack on the Constitution.

"The First Amendment right to free speech does not apply only to agreeable speech. No matter how much I may disagree with BDS, and find it strategically stupid and morally repugnant, I will always fight to protect Americans’ right to speech with which I disagree," Nadler said in a statement.

Meanwhile, House Rules Committee Chairwoman Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., said BDS policies at colleges created hostile environments by "marginalizing Jewish students." She said it was the government's duty to protect the equal rights of those students, who she argued were living in a hostile environment at schools with anti-Israel policies.

CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM EXTENDS BEYOND STUDENT PROTESTS AND INTO CLASSROOMS, ADL WARNS

"They are discriminating against people of the Jewish faith," Foxx said. "Now is not the time for talk. It is the time for action."

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., said during debate on the bill that it was Jewish students who were often leading BDS movements on college campuses.

"This is an attack on free speech and academic freedom, all in the name of defending a genocidal apartheid state," Tlaib said. "A vote for this bill is a betrayal of those promising young students...because they want to save lives, no matter their faith or ethnicity."

item.title: Minneapolis apartment shooting suspect was facing eviction: report
item.description: Carlton Neal Johnson II was identified in media reports as the suspected gunman in a shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
The suspected gunman in a shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building that left two people dead and three police officers injured was identified as a 35-year-old resident who was facing eviction from the property, reports said.

Sources identified the individual as Carlton Neal Johnson II, according to Fox9 Minneapolis. The station reported that the suspect, who also died during the shooting, had lived at the Shoreline Plaza apartment complex since March 2025.

Court records obtained by Fox9 Minneapolis reportedly said Johnson was facing eviction for previously making threatening statements.

The records alleged Johnson assaulted another resident on the property in March, and in mid-June, he "walked around the premises with a firearm openly displayed" and entered the building’s management office, where he displayed the weapon to multiple personnel there, the station reported.

3 DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECTED GUNMAN, AND 3 OFFICERS INJURED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING

Johnson also allegedly made statements to other residents that he had obtained a new firearm and "would kill someone," Fox9 Minneapolis reported.

However, Johnson reportedly denied the allegations in the eviction proceedings and a court date had been set for Sept. 11.

Interim Minneapolis Police Chief Bill Peterson said investigators were "familiar with who this individual was," but did not reveal a motive for Wednesday’s shooting, according to The Minnesota Star Tribune.

The newspaper reported that Johnson was linked to 34 criminal cases in the Twin Cities. It described most of the cases as traffic violations, but added that Johnson previously was charged in two assaults and two misdemeanor drug cases.

Johnson also pled guilty in 2012 to violating a contact order in a domestic abuse case, The Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

MINNEAPOLIS MAYOR'S VIRAL HIP-HOP MOVES SPARK 'HUMILIATION RITUAL' MOCKERY ONLINE

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Minneapolis Police Department for comment.

Minneapolis Police Department Sgt. Garrett Parten said at a news conference on Wednesday that it's unclear how the suspected gunman died.

"Initial information indicated that one person had been shot, and additional 911 callers reported hearing further gunfire. Officers began arriving at approximately 4:39 p.m. and entered the high-rise apartment building," Parten said. "Inside, officers encountered victims and heard additional gunfire. Officers followed the sound of gunfire to the upper floor of the building and on that floor, officers encountered a haze that significantly limited their visibility. Three officers were injured, two of those by gunfire."

item.title: Good Good CEO and president step down amid controversial ad drama following late-night bashing of Callaway
item.description: Good Good golf CEO Matt Kendrick and president Joe Flannery are both out after the controversial Callaway ad fallout that rocked the golf world.
item.content:encoded:
The drama and fallout involving Good Good golf and its controversial ad have developed into what feels like a never-ending story, and the latest chapter involves two figures seated at the top of the brand's pyramid stepping down.

President Joe Flannery, who had only been in the role for a few days when the advertisement was published, is stepping down. CEO and co-founder Matt Kendrick is also out after publicly calling out Callaway after the company cut ties with Good Good following the advertisement.

According to Business Insider, Good Good's leader of operations and finance, Alex Puchala, shared the news in a memo sent to the company on Wednesday while also announcing that co-founder Nahid Giga is stepping into an interim CEO role.

GOOD GOOD GOLF DOESN'T DESERVE TO BE CANCELED FOR THEIR DUMB AD IN COLLABORATION WITH CALLAWAY

Good Good, the wildly popular YouTube channel and golf apparel brand, teamed up with Callaway in late August and collaborated on a new driver. To promote the new equipment, Good Good shared an advertisement in which co-founder Garrett Clark shoved a female member of the brand to the ground.

YOUTUBE GOLFER GRANT HORVAT IS SELLING KIDS GOLF CLUBS WITH AN ALARMINGLY HIGH PRICE TAG

The ad was deleted, and multiple apologetic statements were made by Good Good and Callaway, but the consequences have been severe. Callaway ended its partnership with Good Good, the brand split with the PGA Tour ahead of its sponsored tournament set for November, plus Good Good apparel has been pulled from the shelves at multiple retailers, among other ramifications.

Callaway announced in a statement from CEO Chip Brewer that the "content review process was not comprehensive enough," and they have taken "appropriate internal corrective actions and significantly strengthened our approval procedures to help ensure this does not happen again."

Callaway admitted in its statement that it greenlit the advertisement before it was shared online, and that, coupled with the company deciding to end its partnership with Good Good, led to Kendrick bashing the major golf manufacturer online.

"Interesting that @CallawayGolf asks us to make an ad then approves it then asks us to take the fall then drops us in a coordinated media blitz and covers it up by giving a million dollars away thinking everyone will be ok with it," Kendrick wrote on X at 3:38 AM ET on August 28.

Kendrick also posted on X that he was "not opposed" to suing Callaway while replying to another post on the social media app, but has since deleted the post.

Good Good, which has over 2 million subscribers on YouTube, has resumed sharing new content on its channel in recent days.

item.title: Trey Gowdy opens up about the hidden toll of becoming a great prosecutor
item.description: Trey Gowdy reveals the emotional toll of his prosecutorial career and recalls encounters with David Smith from the infamous Susan Smith murder case.
item.content:encoded:
For Trey Gowdy, the best prosecutors don't simply prove their case, they make a jury feel it themselves.

"The best prosecutors are the ones that can make the jury feel what the parents feel," Gowdy said on the latest episode of the "Hang Out With Sean Hannity" podcast.

"And that's what takes its toll. It wrecks you. It wrecks you," he added.

HOW TO WATCH THE 'HANG OUT WITH SEAN HANNITY' PODCAST

Gowdy, now a Fox News host, sat down with Hannity for a wide-ranging conversation reflecting on the skills and emotional toll behind a prosecutorial career in which he never lost a case.

For Gowdy, connecting with a jury meant first finding a way to understand the anguish of the people at the center of a case.

"Having children helps because you imagine, what if they were taken from you? Having a spouse helps," Gowdy said. "But some folks, I think either are born with or can acquire this empathetic gene, where they can communicate that anguish and pain."

But one case he recalled offered an especially haunting reminder of the grief that remains long after a prosecution ends.

FATHER RECALLS HORROR AFTER SON MURDERED HIS 5 GRANDCHILDREN: ‘I KNEW HE KILLED THEM’

He recalled regularly encountering David Smith, whose two young sons were drowned by their mother, Susan Smith, in a notorious 1994 South Carolina murder case.

"The father of those two boys worked at the grocery store where I shopped, Saturday mornings," Gowdy said. "And I made a point of always speaking to him and never mentioning the case. We talked sports."

"But if you want to see grief etched in someone's face, it was etched in his," he continued. "To lose your two sons because your wife decided that she wanted to have a different boyfriend."

The encounters with Smith offered Gowdy a firsthand glimpse of the anguish he says prosecutors must somehow convey to jurors while remaining composed enough to make their case.

"You've got to marshal the evidence, you've got to stay composed long enough to prevent it, and then this marriage of logic and passion is what closing argument is, this marriage, of moving people," he added.

Gowdy's full discussion with Hannity is available on iHeartRadio, YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.title: Powerful union leader backs Republican in key Senate showdown
item.description: Sean O'Brien, one of the top union leaders in the country, backed Sen. Roger Marshall in the Kansas Senate race against Democrat Adam Hamilton.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: One of the top union leaders in the country has waded into a key Senate contest, backing the Republican incumbent in a race that could determine the balance of power in the upper chamber.

Teamsters General President Sean O’Brien is backing Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., in his bid for re-election as Republicans look to solidify their grip in the upper chamber and push back against the headwinds that browbeat the party in power during a midterm election cycle.

"Sen. Marshall has proven time and time again that he is a friend of labor," O’Brien said in a statement first obtained by Fox News Digital. "As a member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, Sen. Marshall has been eager to partner with us on legislation that protects workers, even when it requires breaking rank with his own party."

EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP-BACKED CHALLENGER GAINS LABOR UNION SUPPORT IN KEY RACE FOR HOUSE CONTROL

"We look forward to continuing to work together with Sen. Marshall to fight for the rights of hardworking Americans," he continued.

O’Brien’s green light to Marshall comes as Teamsters Local 696, the Topeka, Kansas-based chapter of the Teamsters, also threw its support behind the lawmaker, who is seeking a second term in the Senate.

"We are proud to endorse the candidate in this race who continues to be a voice for the middle-class workers of our great state, and that candidate is Sen. Marshall," Local 696 President Mike Scribner said in a statement.

"Kansas Teamsters need someone in Washington who is willing to fight on their behalf," he continued. "Throughout his tenure, Sen. Marshall has shown that he is the person for the job."

O’Brien has morphed into a notable figure in the GOP after his appearance as one of the opening speakers at the Republican National Convention in 2024.

'LET'S BREW IT IN THE UNITED STATES': TEAMSTERS TARGET MODELO AND CORONA IN PUSH FOR MEXICAN BEER TARIFFS

He also formed a political alliance and friendship with one of President Donald Trump’s top allies, Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and even backed Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s nomination to the job after nearly coming to blows with the Trump official two years prior.

It’s Marshall’s backing of pro-labor bills, like Hawley’s Faster Labor Contracts Act, and Sen. Ed Markey’s, D-Mass., Warehouse Worker Protection Act and his own Railway Safety Act that scored him the backing of the Teamsters. He also led the Overtime Wages Relief Act, which eliminated federal income tax on up to $10,000 of overtime wages for individuals and $20,000 for married filers as part of Trump's "one big, beautiful bill."

Marshall is running against Kansas Senate Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton, the lead pastor of the state’s largest Methodist megachurch. Kansas is a ruby-red stronghold, meaning national Republicans aren’t rushing to aid the incumbent in warding off Hamilton.

FOUR MONTHS TO MIDTERMS: 12 RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE THE SENATE MAJORITY

Still, Hamilton has already proven a deft fundraiser, nearly matching Marshall’s war chest in a fraction of the time.

Hamilton has so far raised just north of $4.1 million, while Marshall has brought in just over $6.2 million in a race that Cook Political Report has rated as "likely Republican."

But Hamilton will have to battle both a strong incumbent and history to have a chance at the seat. That’s because Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century. The last time was in the 1930s, when Kansans elected former Sen. George McGill. He only served one term before being ousted by a Republican.

item.title: Maduro claims immunity, asks judge to dismiss drug-trafficking charges against him and his wife
item.description: Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores argue sovereign immunity shields them from narco-terrorism and drug trafficking charges in a federal motion to dismiss.
item.content:encoded:
Former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores asked a federal judge Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking charges against them, arguing, among other things, that the pair have sovereign immunity, according to court documents.

"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought. That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own," a memorandum Maduro's lawyers filed in support of their motion to dismiss read.

"That immunity flows not from goodwill that can be withdrawn on a whim, but from the perfect equality and absolute independence of sovereigns. Thus, this Court lacks jurisdiction with respect to Mr. Maduro, who is recognized by the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela as its head of state," the document continued.

MADURO ALLY DEPORTED TO US OVER ALLEGED BILLION-DOLLAR CORRUPTION SCHEME TIED TO OIL, FOOD PROGRAM

In January 2026, the United States Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York unsealed a fourth superseding indictment against Maduro and Flores. The indictment charged Maduro with narco-terrorism conspiracy, and both Flores and Maduro with cocaine importation conspiracy, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

The indictment alleged that for decades, Maduro used his position — first as a deputy in Venezuela's National Assembly and then as the country's president — to conspire with narco-terrorists from some of the world's largest cartels to import cocaine into the United States.

Maduro's lawyers, however, claim that sovereign immunity prevents the U.S. from taking action against Maduro.

"The official character of these acts — such as issuing diplomatic passports, deploying the military, and announcing Venezuelan foreign policy — is apparent from the face of the Indictment. Because these actions were undertaken in his official capacity on behalf of a foreign sovereign, he may not be required to respond in this Court to the Indictment’s characterizations of his motives and intent in taking these actions," the document reads.

STATE DEPARTMENT ANNOUNCES 'TOTAL COMPLIANCE' FROM VENEZUELAN GOVERNMENT IN RELIEF EFFORTS AFTER MADURO ARREST

The U.S. government officially declared Maduro to be an illegitimate president in 2019 after Maduro declared victory in the disputed 2018 presidential election.

Maduro's lawyers also argue that the indictment violates his and Flores' due process, according to court documents.

The document asserts that Maduro "vehemently denies that he had anything to do with drug trafficking or intended to benefit anyone engaged in terrorism."

The motion to dismiss then argues that the charges against Maduro fail to establish that his alleged crimes took place in or were aimed at the United States, and therefore do not meet the standards of due process.

ARMY SOLDIER INVOLVED IN MADURO CAPTURE ARRESTED FOR ALLEGEDLY USING CLASSIFIED INTEL TO WIN $410K IN BETS

"The narcoterrorism statute, which was enacted in 2006 in connection with the reauthorization of the USA PATRIOT ACT, was intended to target foreign conduct. Recognizing that its power to police the rest of the world is not unlimited, Congress included a jurisdictional element that authorizes the use of the statute to prosecute foreign conduct under only five enumerated scenarios in which the foreign conduct is connected to the United States. Ignoring those parameters set by Congress, the Indictment fails — even by tracking the statutory language — to allege any basis for jurisdiction over the solely foreign conduct it alleges," the motion to dismiss reads.

The U.S. apprehended Maduro and Flores during a January military operation, titled Operation Absolute Resolve, in which U.S. forces captured the couple in Venezuela's capital of Caracas and extradited them back to the United States to be prosecuted in New York federal court.

TRUMP PICKS JAMES MCDONALD TO LEAD POWERFUL SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK AFTER JAY CLAYTON'S DEPARTURE

Maduro is set to appear in court in November to begin oral arguments in support of his motion to dismiss.

Fox News Digital contacted Maduro and Flores' legal team and the SDNY for further comment.

item.title: The ultimate college football tailgate playlist with 10 songs to get fired up for the season
item.description: From "Country Roads" to "Enter Sandman," this top-10 college football tailgate playlist covers rock anthems and country classics for pregame.
item.content:encoded:
College football is officially in full swing, and that means it's time for the ultimate playlist to get fired up.

Thursday night features several games to wet the whistle before a packed Saturday of action and games Sunday and Monday.

If you're not excited, then I have to wonder if you're a patriotic American.

Of course, we all know you can't have college football season without the tailgates and parties that are mandatory.

Top priority:

14 TAILGATING ESSENTIALS FOR GRILLING, WATCHING THE GAME AND STAYING WARM

A fire playlist.

Well, you're all in luck because I have you all taken care of to make sure you don't miss a single hit for your tailgate/pregame playlist.

Now, we'd be here for days if I listed every song that needs to be included. What I'm going to do is give you a surefire top-10 hit list.

Let's roll.

1) John Denver - Take Me Home, Country Roads

Easiest choice ever. No hesitation. No thought about it. If you're not a fan of this song, then you're not a fan of America. It's an all-time classic and perfectly captures the feeling of fall weather and good vibes.

2) Toby Keith - Courtesy Of The Red, White And Blue

Toby Keith (RIP) made several monster hits during his career, but this one stands out as the most iconic. It will have you ready to run through a wall.

3) AC/DC - Hells Bells

Is there a song with a more recognizable opening few seconds than "Hells Bells"? I think the answer is no, and it only takes off from there. It's pure adrenaline start to finish.

4) AC/DC - Thunderstruck

Speaking of AC/DC, I can't include one of their songs without also including "Thunderstruck." Another all-time classic that is great for football season and any and all tailgates and pregames.

5) Alice In Chains - Man in the Box

Sticking with some rock music, there is no chance "Man in the Box" by Alice in Chains isn't making my tailgate playlist. There are probably six other Alice in Chains songs that I will have as well, but "Man in the Box" is another example of pure adrenaline. "Rooster" is also in high consideration.

6) Metallica - Enter Sandman

Where are all my Virginia Tech fans at? It might be Virginia Tech's entrance song, but this song fits in perfectly in just about any sports setting. You simply can't go wrong with "Enter Sandman."

7) Alabama - Song of the South

Switching gears, "Song of the South" is an anthem for people in the South, and it's not hard to see why. The song is an absolute classic from Alabama. Is there a single fan above the age of 40 at a Georgia, Ole Miss, LSU, Alabama or Auburn tailgate who doesn't have this on their playlist? I think the answer is no.

8) House of Pain - Jump Around

As a Wisconsin man, this song is about as on-brand as it gets. It's played between the third and fourth quarters at Camp Randall, and the stadium shakes to the point you can feel it outside and water inside the stadium literally vibrates.

9) Guns N' Roses - Welcome to the Jungle

Another all-time rock classic that you simply can't go wrong with by blasting it under a tent as the sun beats down ahead of kickoff.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

10) Gordon Lightfoot - Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald

This might seem like it's totally out of left field, but what you have to understand is that people in the Midwest love "Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald." The Mighty Fitz went down in 1975, and has lived on in Midwestern legend ever since. If there's one song that unites people across all backgrounds and ages in the Great Lakes region of the Midwest, it's this classic from Gordon Lightfoot.

Do you have a favorite song you always smash the play button on during football season? Let me know at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

item.description: Thursday Screencaps celebrates a reader's 50-year love story that began with a chance encounter at a Toledo Ramada Inn and a shared passion for golf.
item.content:encoded:
After battling the crud last weekend and early this week, I'm happy to say that I'm working at 90% for this edition of Thursday Screencaps. Thank you to those who have reached out during this difficult time. I was facing the possibility of not being able to sit on the patio this weekend to watch football, swim, suck down beers and enjoy summer.

The football gods intervened. They weren't having it. There's golf to play with Screencaps Jr. There are garden tours to do with Mrs. Screencaps. Folks, I'M BACK (enough).

Let's get rolling this morning ... remember Wednesday Screencaps where I challenged you guys to tell me about pivot points in your life? I was blown away by some of the responses. Truly. I'm constantly shocked by the intellectual level of people who care about this column, which was created approximately 15 years ago to be a column for sports-loving degenerates. Instead, even though I haven't changed the format, Screencaps has morphed into a daily dose of reality for intellectuals, degenerates and those of us who are just seeking out an authentic part of the internet where real conversations are being had.

WHAT THE DALLAS COWBOYS CHEERLEADERS MAKE PER GAME MIGHT SURPRISE YOU, GOTTERUP LOVES THE USA & LIFE PIVOTS

– Steven S., a "career investigator," emails: I always enjoy reading your stories. I particularly love the parts about how you discuss your $10 URL and how it changed your life. I enjoy collecting stories from how people have changed their lives from a seemingly mundane decision. My question to you is have you ever thought about writing a manuscript or book about your own career for others to follow and read? I would be interested in hearing more about this career transformation.

Kinsey: I look at the Screencaps archive as being the book on my career. At this point, the book has something like 5,000 pages. Maybe more. I've always thought books were reserved for really important people. Personally, I've never wanted to be published book important. The genesis of this column and my career came out of the troubling economic times of 2008-2010-11. My work was always about helping people forget about divorces they were going through, jobs they were losing and lives that just weren't going the right way.

LAWYER-TURNED-SOCIAL MEDIA SENSATION IS BETTING IT ALL ON GOD, LOVE AND GRIEF

Steven, maybe I just need someone like you to guide me here. What do people want to hear about in a book?

– GDaddy shares a story from his own personal book and it's a perfectly-timed email: Choosing a new fork in the road. On January 26, 1976, I was living in Cleveland and was in Toledo on business and having dinner and a couple of beers at a Ramada Inn on Reynolds Road. We were talking business for along timeand ultimately a young lady from Waterville, Ohio came to our table and asked us what was so interesting after first apologiing for interrupting us. Short story, we didn't know it was 'Monday Night Singles Night" and that a band was going to start playing soon.

AN OPEN MARRIAGE SOMEHOW LEADS TO REGRET, WOMAN HOOKS BEST FRIEND UP WITH SISTER'S EX & DUMB DIVORCE EXCUSES

I was 33 at the time and divorced, my boss was a couple of ;years older than me and the lady from Waterville was 24 and her Owens Illinois co-worker was a couple of years older and they were single with no kids. We had a couple of beverages with them, and may have danced a dance, I got a phone number before us two guys headed off to our rooms. Could have been end of story. . .

I was going to be in Toledo again on Feb 5, and I called "Miss Waterville" to see if she might like to have dinner on the 5th and she said something like,"I guess so". . . We had dinner, and there was a big snowstorm, and could have been end of story again. . .

(condensed version now) . We started dating and we decided to get an apartment together in mid-April adjacent to Brandywine. I'd competed in golf for several years and we started playing golf together (and we still play now at 83 and 74). On August 22, 1976 we were having dinner at The Charcoal House which used to be at 4031 Talmadge Rd (I know that from looking at the receipt that we had framed). My wife-to-be said "let's get married" (thinking that I wasn't going to be accommodating).

I said "OK" and the next question from her was "when?" I thought it over briefly and then said, "How about next Friday night after golf league?"

She looked a little stunned but said she would call her minister the next morning and she would start making whatever plans needed to really be made. I said that I would talk with the guys running the league and make sure that my partner and I would get the first tee time at 5:00PM so that we could get the "ceremony" done and then have a dinner down on the River. As it turned out, her minister was on vacation the following week and she had to get another minister to unite us. My best man was my golf partner (a young lawyer), our team won our match on Friday night at Riverby Hills, and we got married and had a nice dinner on the Maumee.

That was 50 years ago today, September 3, 1976. We had a fabulous honeymoon attending the World Series of Golf in Akron, and also going to Cedar Point.

Golf is something you can do for a lifetime, and you're usually playing it with friends and having a good time. Nobody gets in the clubhouse and starts talking about their bad shots---it's all about the good shots each of us hit. Over the years we've attended lots of great golf tournaments, starting with the initial Memorial Tournament in'76.

Been to the Masters, President's Cup, PGA, US Open, the first 12 Tour Championships (the company I worked for in Atlanta was one of the original sponsors), and we've gotten to play some fabulous golf courses.

AIR FORCE RESCINDING 135 PROMOTIONS AFTER TEST SCORING ERROR: 'THIS IS GOING TO BE HARD'

I could go on and on and brag about my kids and my 8 grand kids (5 of 8 live in Ohio) but let me finish by saying that the "fork in the road" was there in January 1976, and a young lady from Waterville Ohio came over to interrupt a couple of business-talking guys, and that road that was taken gets better and better every single moment of every year that has gone by. It's our Love Story. . . . and I definitely out-kicked my coverage!

Kinsey: Happy anniversary, GDaddy. Now I need to figure out a way to play 18 with GDaddy. The guy is 83 and seems like one of the guys and probably pumps bombs right down the middle to the 150 stake.

THE BEST BACK-TO-SCHOOL DEALS OF 2026: LAPTOPS, BACKPACKS, DORM ESSENTIALS AND MORE

– Pat R., MD (a real doctor of medicine) emails: I follow your columns regularly and enjoy them tremendously, but your column about the "zigs" in our lives, those moments that end up defining everything that comes afterward, really resonated with me.

It made me stop for a minute and think about my own life, and I realized I know exactly what my zig was.

In 1996, I was 35 years old (oh so young! hehe), the mother of 4 children. My youngest was only six months old and I decided to go to medical school. Looking back, it sounds somewhat crazy even to me. I had a whole list of sensible reasons not to do it. But it was my dream, so I did it.

With it came sacrifices for me and the family but also many rewards. This decision led to a career as a medical oncologist that has been extraordinarily satisfying. I have had the privilege of caring for people during some of the most difficult moments of their lives, participating in research, building programs, and doing work that, after all these years, I still love.

Your column made me realize something: becoming a physician was not really the defining moment. Graduating from medical school wasn't either.

The defining moment was being a 35 year old mother of 4, and deciding to take the zig of a lifetime. Everything else followed from that.

Thank you for writing something that made me look back at my own life from a different angle.

Kinsey: I did my due diligence on Pat R. and realized just how important her pivot was and what it meant for the world of medicine. I'm truly honored that Pat R. even cares what's written in Screencaps. I don't mean that as a slight to the degenerate businessmen who read this column while slamming drinks in airport lounges. I respect you guys, too, but Pat R. has done some cancer work that is personal for me.

Pat, I have no idea what made you want to read, but I'm happy to have you.

– James Mc shares his life pivot point where everything changed: So, so easy for me. 1983, Sitting in the living room of an economy apartment (that also doubled as the bedroom) with a group of friends, staring at the apartment's resident. He was a 24- or 25-year-old Ice Cream Shop manager (a future Al Bundy if ever there was one) passing out beer as he mesmerized several of the naive 17- and 18-year-old girls in attendance with tales of his fabulous job.

It was at that very moment that I realized, "Oh my God, that is going to be me in just a few short years!" Hopefully, moving up the ranks at our local grocery store from sacker, to cashier, to stocker, or perhaps even an assistant manager one day.

By the end of the evening, I'd made up my mind. I hopped in my 1976 Datsun B-210 and headed across town to the military enlistment center where I slept for the remainder of the night. Military recruiters' days begin early, and I was waiting for them. I boldly marched into the Air Force recruiting office and announced I was ready to join-up (hang-over and all). Several hours of paperwork later, I was on my way. It took an additional six weeks to finalize everything, but I was finally off to boot camp and an adventure that would span the next 21 years.

During that time, I would meet my future wife (also Air Force) at Rhein Main Air Force Base, Germany and be married less than 6 months later in Denmark. We would be stationed at an additional 8 Air Force Bases both overseas and in-country throughout my career, survive two terrorist bombings, two major hurricanes, and adopt our 2 beautiful daughters.

It was one heck of a ride, and all thanks to a 24- or -25-year old Ice Cream Shop manager!

– Scott W.'s pivot point started with getting sober: Your column on $10 URLs and life pivots hit right where it needed to for me this morning.

My pivot didn't start in a pristine office, it started in a stretch in rehab for the sauce. I was sitting there, coding away on a computer with zero internet connection, just trying to keep my head clear and build something real. During one of the only two family visits I was allowed the entire time, I managed to sneak away just long enough to jump online and register a domain name, the one I have emailed you from.

I already had 20 years of software engineering behind me, solving problems for plenty of big companies. But this time, I was fighting for my own life, and building something I actually believed in and was mine.

When I got out, I aligned with a co-founder who went through the thick of it with me. We raised money, set off to build the business, and well... I stayed sober.

For ten long years, almost everyone in my circle treated the whole thing like a punchline, even as I made massive gains in my day job, my dream to them was a joke. That quick, snuck-in domain purchase in the middle of rehab didn't just spawn a company, it anchored my recovery and completely reshaped the rest of my life over the last 10 years of trying to prove my thoughts were valid. No fanfare, no bragging, no "I told you so" back to my critics, just the epic rush of reaching the beachhead of my vision and what's to come....and making mad bank doesn't hurt :) The biggest defining moment, aside from my kids and grandchild, yet.

item.title: When gunman forced his way into Virginia elementary school, superintendent says lockdown procedures worked
item.description: Waynesboro police say a 19-year-old gunman entered Westwood Hills Elementary School and injured a staff member before school lockdown procedures kicked in.
item.content:encoded:
A 19-year-old gunman got inside a Virginia elementary school about 30 miles west of Charlottesville on Wednesday morning, injuring an adult staff member before turning the gun on himself, authorities said during a press conference later that day.

The subject, Anthony Ignatiadis-Isabelle, was found "dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound," Waynesboro Police Chief David Shaw said.

His body was found inside the library of Westwood Hills Elementary School, and no students were inside the library at the time, police said.

Jeffrey Cassell, superintendent of Waynesboro Public Schools, praised the school's lockdown procedures and training, saying they "worked" in a time of crisis.

THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN

"Our safety and security protocols and procedures worked. Staff notified law enforcement immediately, and our school executed lockdown procedures. Every student and staff member is safe and returned home to their families," Cassell said.

"If you don't get emotional today, you never will. Today is the day every school system hopes they never have to deal with," Cassell added, appearing to choke up. "Please hug your children and your families this evening."

Ignatiadis-Isabelle had not attended any school in the district, Cassell told reporters.

VIRGINIA UNIVERSITY REPORT FINDS OFFICIALS DID NOT DISCLOSE STUDENT’S TERROR CONVICTION

Authorities did not share any details about an alleged motive, nor did they reveal anything about the weapon used or if the deceased gunman had a connection to the staff member who suffered a non-life-threatening gunshot wound.

The identity of the staff member, who was treated and released from the hospital, has not been made public.

Police emphasized multiple times throughout the press conference that the investigation remains active and ongoing.

The last school shooting in Virginia occurred on Aug. 15 at Virginia State University in Chesterfield County. Five students were left injured and the suspect, 19-year-old Camron Harris, was arrested the same day after police said officers found him hiding in a closet inside one of the campus dorm buildings.

item.title: America mocked the Amish and other groups over technology. Maybe they were right
item.description: As Meta settled for up to $17 billion over claims its platforms harmed children, Hasidic smartphone restrictions started looking less backward.
item.content:encoded:
The irony was hard to miss last week. The same day that a documentary (with more than 35 million views as of Sept. 2) portrayed Hasidic restrictions on smartphones and the internet as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a proposed settlement worth up to $17 billion with a coalition of states over allegations that Facebook and Instagram harmed children through addictive design. Meta denies wrongdoing.

As a kid, I spent enormous amounts of time outdoors, growing up near the Santa Monica Mountains and later in the rural mountains of Tehachapi, California. I explored the hills, watched wildlife, fished, stared at the stars, listened to coyotes howl and loved sleeping outside so much that sending me indoors for the night was my punishment.

Try that punishment on a child with a smartphone today. A bedroom can contain a universe more compelling than anything outside: social media, YouTube, video games, group chats and an infinite stream of entertainment engineered to keep us hooked. When our oldest daughter was one year old, she became so attached to her iPad Mini that she’d shake her crib, crying, "iPad! iPad! iPad!" when we took it away.

WE GREW UP BEFORE SCREENS TOOK OVER. OUR KIDS DESERVE THAT CHANCE TOO

In his documentary, Turkish filmmaker Ruhi Çenet takes viewers inside Hasidic communities in New York. Again and again, their distance from modern technology helps establish just how unusual and insular their world appears.

"Have you ever watched television?" Çenet asks one man. "Have you ever logged into the internet in your entire life?"

He learns that some members regard unrestricted internet access as dangerous to religious life. Some use "kosher" phones stripped of texting, web browsers and social media. Computers needed for work use filters restricting which websites users can visit. Instead of mainstream social media, some communities maintain telephone networks where people listen to stories, religious teachings and inspirational content.

Looking at one kosher phone, Çenet marvels: "There’s no way to send SMS. No way to search anything. It’s like a walkie-talkie." Later, he remarks, "It feels like I traveled back in time," his stunned tone framing these restrictions as inherently negative.

JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIAL MEDIA ADDICTION WILL EASILY OUTLAST META'S MASSIVE MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR SETTLEMENT

Then, on the same day that viewers of Çenet’s documentary encountered religious restrictions on technology as evidence of a backward, insular world, Meta agreed to a settlement, still subject to court approval, that would impose restrictions of its own, including a default daily limit for teens, blocking access overnight and adopting other safeguards aimed at reducing compulsive use.

Perhaps the remarkable thing about a phone that "only makes calls" isn’t how little it can do. Perhaps it’s how little it can do to you.

BIG TECH IS THROUGH HARMING OUR CHILDREN. THIS IS OUR TIME TO FIGHT BACK

We routinely describe communities such as the Amish and some Jewish, Christian and Muslim groups as insular because they resist technologies that everyone else embraces.

Last week, for instance, California’s Catholic bishops backed AB 1709, legislation that would restrict covered platforms from providing addictive features to children under 16. While the legislation has not yet become law, that resistance can still look irrational from the outside. Why reject a device capable of placing nearly all human knowledge in your pocket?

AS AI RESHAPES DATING, A JEWISH ORGANIZATION IS BETTING ON THE RETURN OF THE HUMAN MATCHMAKER

Of course, practices vary enormously. Some communities heavily restrict internet access; Chabad Lubavitch, the Hasidic movement with which I identify, embraces the internet as a tool for Jewish education and outreach.

The lesson isn’t that these communities discovered the perfect technologies to prohibit. It’s that they believed they had the right to ask what technology would do to them before adopting it.

'IF WI-FI WENT OUT TOMORROW – CHAOS': AMERICAN ADDICTION TO TECHNOLOGY EXPLORED ON 'PLANET TYRUS'

Modern America mostly reversed the process. We asked what technology could do for us first and worried about what it was doing to us later.

We handed children extraordinarily sophisticated attention-capturing machines and then seemed surprised when they struggled to put them down.

IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT?

The U.S. Surgeon General’s office now calls harm from screen use among children and adolescents a public-health concern. Recent research has linked smartphone and screen use to depression, insufficient sleep and other adverse health outcomes. A 2026 Pediatrics study of 10,588 U.S. children found that smartphone ownership at age 12 was associated with higher odds of depression, obesity and insufficient sleep, although it’s important to note that the observational study could not establish causation.

Researchers continue to debate causation, individual vulnerability and which forms of screen use cause the greatest harm. But handing children unrestricted access to products deliberately engineered to capture attention amounted to an enormous social experiment.

PHONE-FREE RESTAURANTS ARE TRENDING ACROSS THE US

And we ran the experiment before knowing the results. Now mainstream society is trying to recreate boundaries that traditional communities never abandoned.

Phone-free schools. Devices outside bedrooms. Parental controls. Delayed smartphones. Screen-time limits. Social media age restrictions. Notifications disabled overnight.

Practices that once looked like symptoms of religious insularity have acquired respectable secular names: digital wellness, screen hygiene and intentional technology.

Insularity carries genuine dangers. Communities that severely restrict outside information can suppress dissent, conceal abuse and limit access to ideas and opportunities. We should never romanticize that.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

But isolation and restraint are not the same thing. The Amish preserve face-to-face communal life and manual work. Hasidic communities center life heavily around family, synagogue, schools, religious study and communal gatherings. Orthodox Judaism gives me something even more radical: Shabbat.

For roughly 25 hours every week, my phone stops buzzing. Emails wait. Work stops. In our hyperconnected world, deliberately making yourself unreachable sounds restrictive. I experience it as freedom.

We tend to define technological freedom as more access, information, entertainment and choice. But the freedom to be unavailable is another kind of freedom. To be bored. To sit through dinner without checking who texted. To walk through the woods. To let children experience an afternoon without an algorithm deciding what should capture attention.

I don’t want to abandon modernity. Technology allows me to work, learn and maintain relationships in ways my grandparents could scarcely have imagined. The lesson isn’t to become Amish or Hasidic. It is to start with a hierarchy of values such as family, faith and community, and then ask where technology fits.

When I was a child, being sent inside felt like punishment because the world I wanted was outside. Today, parents often fight the opposite battle: getting children to put down their devices and walk outside.

For years, we looked at people without smartphones and wondered what they were missing. Perhaps we should have spent more time asking what they were preserving. Not every boundary is a prison. Sometimes it protects what matters most.
